messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] achieving Hello World
messages.body_plain:
[cc-ing stan-dev]

I believe the direct answer to Scott Akenhead's query is that
you need to install Rcpp from source (why, I have no idea --- I'm
not an R expert or Rcpp expert).

Does anyone on the dev team understand all the combinatorics
of R / Mac / Rcpp / compilers to the point where we can provide
better instructions.  The instructions that are there worked for
me as written no problem, so I can't even recreate the trouble our
users seem to be getting themselves into.

Can someone (preferably Ben or Jiqiang who have some chance of
getting it right) update our install instructions for RStan on
Mavericks on the wiki?  We're getting lots of e-mail like this,
and it's starting to freak me out that we're going to be losing
R users who can't get through our patchwork install instructions.

I believe the issues we're having are the new ones introduced
by the interaction of Rcpp and Mavericks and the new Xcode, all
of which changed out from under us (not that this helps our
poor users struggling with installs).

Scott --- how did you figure out how to edit the .R directory?
It's trivial if you have a text editor (like emacs), but I'm curious
as to how you were trying to do it and finally managed to do it so
we can help others who don't use text editors.
Andrew had the same problem --- said he had no idea how to edit
a file starting with ".".    It never even occurred to me that
this could be a point of failure, but now we know and should help
people out.

I don't have time now, but after two weeks, I'm willing to be
a guinea pig and completely rip out my C++ compilers and R installs
and start from scratch.

- Bob

On Jun 4, 2014, at 9:43 AM, Scott Akenhead <sc...@s4s.com> wrote:

> The previous version of RStan installed on the previous version of R with zero fussing, and I did cool Bayesian models quickly. Loved it.
> But with  Mac OS X 10.9.3, installing RStan has been 20 miles of bad road.
> The RStan Getting Started guide instructed me to create ~/.R/Makevars with exactly these two lines:
>       CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++
>       CXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"
> This was tricky because I had to create ~/.R and to do that I had to make Mac Finder show hidden files. That was not straightforward.
> The script proffered to do this does not work if ~/.R does not exist. Not having  ~/.R  was disconcerting.
> Getting Started also instructed me to install Xcode 5.1.1 in order to have a C++ compiler. Some web searching revealed the trick where you run Xcode separately to accept the Apple license. And there is something about setting “Command Line Tools” in Xcode > Downloads so that refers to Xcode 5.1.1, except that seems to be Xcode > Locations, but it looks OK.
> Next I updated Rcpp and inline. I also reinstalled R because I was starting to get nervous.
> Then I tried the Hello World script. FAIL.
> Well, it seems to run Rcpp OK, then quits at the compile stage with this message:
> Compilation argument:
> /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/bin/R CMD SHLIB file1dd173a89f7e.cpp 2> file1dd173a89f7e.cpp.err.txt
> g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++ -I/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/include -DNDEBUG  -I/usr/local/include -I/usr/local/include/freetype2 -I/opt/X11/include -I"/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.1/Resources/library/Rcpp/include"   -fPIC  "-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion" -c file1dd173a89f7e.cpp -o file1dd173a89f7e.o
> g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++ -dynamiclib -Wl,-headerpad_max_install_names -undefined dynamic_lookup -single_module -multiply_defined suppress -L/usr/local/lib -o file1dd173a89f7e.so file1dd173a89f7e.o -F/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/.. -framework R -Wl,-framework -Wl,CoreFoundation
> Looks like it found Makevars OK, given the references to g++. But Xcode supplies the clang compiler. I am guessing there was no g++ so the script just ended, silently.
> I seem to recall that R is compiled with clang, so now I am worrying about compatibility.
> Not that I wanted to go there, but file.show("/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/etc/Makeconf") shows CC = clang and CXX = clang++.
> Anyway, at this point I am forced to call for help.
> Do I install g++ or should I throw away ~/.R/Makevars, ignore the Hello World test, and hope RStan works with clang?
> To compile RStan, do I need g++ or is clang the right way?
>
> My previous and positive experience with Stan led me to tell everyone where I work (fisheries research) to quit using JAGS and BUGS, so please help me get back to evangelizing Stan.
>
>
> --

> For more options, visit https://groups.google.com/d/optout.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] achieving Hello World
messages.body_plain:
Part of the issue is that we have two sets of installation instructions for Macs

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started#how-to-install-rstan
https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Mac-OS-X-Installation-Instructions

The other thing that we at least have control over is the new release. The old release still has the incompatibility with libc++ so you either have to have -stdlib=libstdc++ in CFLAGS or use (llvm-)g++ to install rstan. But (llvm-)g++ doesn't compile models any more, so you have to use clang++ with -stdlib=libstdc++ for that. When we release, it will probably only work with clang++ (or FSF g++) but shouldn't require -stdlib=libstdc++.

CRAN always recommended installing Rcpp from source, but it only seemed to become necessary recently for Stan users who have Macs.

Ben

messages.subject: OperandsAndPartials
messages.body_plain:
I've confused myself again with trying to generalize OperandsAndPartials so it works with forward mode auto-diff. I think the approach I am going to take is to specialize OperandsAndPartials for forward mode such that the prob/distribution files do not need to be changed much at all.

The idea that Daniel and I talked about yesterday was to overload += and -= so when we call something like op_and_p.d_x1[n] += scaled_diff, it would actually result in d_x1 += scaled_diff * x1[n].d_.

In any case, I've confused myself while going through the current OperandsAndPartials code for reverse mode. Namely, in partials_vari.hpp, we have

d_x1(all_partials),
          d_x2(all_partials
               + (!is_constant_struct<T1>::value) * length(x1)),
          d_x3(all_partials
               + (!is_constant_struct<T1>::value) * length(x1)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T2>::value) * length(x2)),
          d_x4(all_partials
               + (!is_constant_struct<T1>::value) * length(x1)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T2>::value) * length(x2)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T3>::value) * length(x3)),
          d_x5(all_partials
               + (!is_constant_struct<T1>::value) * length(x1)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T2>::value) * length(x2)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T3>::value) * length(x3)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T4>::value) * length(x4)),
          d_x6(all_partials
               + (!is_constant_struct<T1>::value) * length(x1)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T2>::value) * length(x2)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T3>::value) * length(x3)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T4>::value) * length(x4)
               + (!is_constant_struct<T5>::value) * length(x5))

but why do we need to create more spaces for d_x2, d_x3, etc. than d_x1? Shouldn't they all end up just being of size N, which is something like

      size_t N = max_size(y, mu, sigma);

messages.subject: Re: OperandsAndPartials
messages.body_plain:
One other thing:

For example in exponential.hpp, we have lines like

      for (size_t n = 0; n < N; n++) {
        const double beta_dbl = value_of(beta_vec[n]);
        const double y_dbl = value_of(y_vec[n]);
        if (include_summand<propto,T_inv_scale>::value)
          logp += log_beta[n];
        if (include_summand<propto,T_y,T_inv_scale>::value)
          logp -= beta_dbl * y_dbl;

        if (!is_constant_struct<T_y>::value)
          operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] -= beta_dbl;
        if (!is_constant_struct<T_inv_scale>::value)
          operands_and_partials.d_x2[n] += 1 / beta_dbl - y_dbl;
      }

but why do we use += and -= and why not just =? Isn't each d_x1[n] and d_x2[n] for n from 0 to N accessed only once? Am I missing something?

RStan install instructions
messages.body_plain:
I think our number one priority for Stan should be
solid R install instructions.  If people can't install
our software, they can't use it.

I think the instructions needs to be of the form where the
user chooses their configuration, then gets step-by-step
instructions with a checklist.

That Mac-OS-X install page was my attempt to do that for
Mac OS, but clearly I didn't succeed and just added to the muddle.
And it wasn't broken out enough by version of Mac OS, etc.

Should I just kill that page?  Or can it be salvaged by fiddling
with the Rcpp instructions?

  https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Mac-OS-X-Installation-Instructions

I'm afraid I'm almost as confused as our users about the dependencies
among Mavericks, Xcode, Rcpp, Windows, installing from source, g++ vs.
clang++, -O0 vs. -O3 and which of those is set automatically by R, and
so on.  And I don't seem to have run into any of the problems Andrew or
our users ran into.

- Bob

On Jun 4, 2014, at 4:08 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Part of the issue is that we have two sets of installation instructions for Macs
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started#how-to-install-rstan
> https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Mac-OS-X-Installation-Instructions
>
> The other thing that we at least have control over is the new release. The old release still has the incompatibility with libc++ so you either have to have -stdlib=libstdc++ in CFLAGS or use (llvm-)g++ to install rstan. But (llvm-)g++ doesn't compile models any more, so you have to use clang++ with -stdlib=libstdc++ for that. When we release, it will probably only work with clang++ (or FSF g++) but shouldn't require -stdlib=libstdc++.
>
> CRAN always recommended installing Rcpp from source, but it only seemed to become necessary recently for Stan users who have Macs.
>
> Ben
>
> On Wednesday, June 4, 2014 4:49:34 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> [cc-ing stan-dev]
>
> I believe the direct answer to Scott Akenhead's query is that
> you need to install Rcpp from source (why, I have no idea --- I'm
> not an R expert or Rcpp expert).
>
> Does anyone on the dev team understand all the combinatorics
> of R / Mac / Rcpp / compilers to the point where we can provide
> better instructions.  The instructions that are there worked for
> me as written no problem, so I can't even recreate the trouble our
> users seem to be getting themselves into.
>
> Can someone (preferably Ben or Jiqiang who have some chance of
> getting it right) update our install instructions for RStan on
> Mavericks on the wiki?  We're getting lots of e-mail like this,
> and it's starting to freak me out that we're going to be losing
> R users who can't get through our patchwork install instructions.
>
> I believe the issues we're having are the new ones introduced
> by the interaction of Rcpp and Mavericks and the new Xcode, all
> of which changed out from under us (not that this helps our
> poor users struggling with installs).
>
> Scott --- how did you figure out how to edit the .R directory?
> It's trivial if you have a text editor (like emacs), but I'm curious
> as to how you were trying to do it and finally managed to do it so
> we can help others who don't use text editors.
> Andrew had the same problem --- said he had no idea how to edit
> a file starting with ".".    It never even occurred to me that
> this could be a point of failure, but now we know and should help
> people out.
>
> I don't have time now, but after two weeks, I'm willing to be
> a guinea pig and completely rip out my C++ compilers and R installs
> and start from scratch.
>
> - Bob

> I think the only problem with that page is that it is less easy to find and that it doesn't work if your Xcode defaults to clang++ with libc++. But the new release should work with that. We should probably change the function at the end to install Rcpp and inline from source to be on the safe side.

One thing about

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Mac-OS-X-Installation-Instructions

is that the last step with the install_rstan() function is ostensibly cross-platform. So we might have a page that is called "Prerequisites for OSX" that would have all that except the last step. And have a similar linked page for how to install Rtools on Windows. And then in the main installation page, have everyone call that install_rstan() function.

Ben

I haven't had time to really dive into the code, but it looks
like the first problem:

  src/stan/agrad/partials_vari.hpp:178:16:
  error: no viable conversion from 'stan::agrad::fvar<double>' to
      'stan::agrad::var'
        return stan::agrad::fvar<T_partials_return>(logp,temp_deriv);
               ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

is because you're returning an agrad::fvar<double>, but the return type,
template param T_return_type is agrad::var.  So you may need to fiddle with
the return type calculation to ensure it matches.  The problem is these
two function signatures:

      T_return_type
      to_var(T_partials_return logp) {
        return partials_to_var<T_return_type>(logp, nvaris, all_varis, all_partials);
      }

      T_return_type
      to_fvar(T_partials_return logp,

They can't both be right, because they both use the same return
type, whereas one returns a var and the other an fvar.

I think you're going to need to write a specialization of OperandsAndPartials
for fvar rather than trying to use a single piece of polymorphic code.

- Bob

Ok, maybe I didn't write the code very clearly. My idea was this:

T_partials_return is double if it's only vars and it's T if the highest order fvar is fvar<T>.

Then, T_return_type is var if all vars and fvar<T> if fvar<T> otherwise (ignoring vectorization for simplicity).

My idea was that only one of either to_var or to_fvar will be needed.

In any case, I tried to specialize OperandsAndPartials but it kept telling me that the second implementation was a redefinition . I also read in the red C++ book that Daniel gave me too look at that there are some issues with some attempts at partial specialization.

Ah.. that sent before I was done.

So I tried something like having the following two

template<typename T1=double, typename T2=double, typename T3=double,

         typename T4=double, typename T5=double, typename T6=double,

         typename T_return_type=typename return_type<T1,T2,T3,T4,T5,T6>::type,

         typename T_partials_return=typename stan::partials_return_type<T1,T2,T3,T4,T5,T6>::type,

bool contain_fvar=stan::contains_fvar<T1,T2,T3,T4,T5,T6>::value>

    struct OperandsAndPartials

and

template<typename T1=double, typename T2=double, typename T3=double,

         typename T4=double, typename T5=double, typename T6=double,

         typename T_return_type=typename return_type<T1,T2,T3,T4,T5,T6>::type,

         typename T_partials_return=typename stan::partials_return_type<T1,T2,T3,T4,T5,T6>::type,

bool contain_fvar=true>
    struct OperandsAndPartials

which gave me the error of redefinition. I'll play around with this some more tomorrow.

messages.body_plain:
You may need to use something like Boost's enable_if to
make sure you don't wind up with multiple instantiations.
You have to make sure that there's a unique most-specific
match.

So you can't have:

  template <typename T> foo(T x, double y);
  template <typename T> foo(double x, T y);

and try to call

  foo(double,double)

because both the declarations match equally well.

But then you can use something like disable_if to ensure
that T in one of the cases is never instantiated if T
is a double.

- Bob

On Jun 6, 2014, at 9:53 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi, Bob.  I put it on stan-dev because non R-users might have thoughts too.

Thanks.

> At some point we can talk about how best to write a spec.  My main thought is to switch to Sebastian's function (or something like it), also to clean up the stan-optimize call and a few other things.

I don't think we need a formal spec process --- just
a simple functional spec consisting of the documentation for
the functions you want to see implemented including examples.
Then, the folks who know R can turn it into a technical spec
that explains how to implement it, but I don't think we
need to formalize a technical spec if the functional spec is solid.

I'll go first with a really informal functional spec just consisting
of examples.  Here's what I would like to see for compilation:

  model <- compile("foo.stan");

for fitting:

  mle_fit <- optimize(model=, data=, ...);
  mcmc_fit <- stan(model=, data=, ...);

and for saving and reloading:

  save_model(model=, file=);
  model <- load_model(file=);

To turn this into a functional spec we can work from,
we have to add descriptions of

  * the rest of the arguments

  * types for each argument

  * return type

  * constraints on legal calling patterns --- the spec has to
    say exactly what arguments require other arguments or disallow
    other arguments, and what sets of legal values there are (this
    is the killer that most R functions don't even bother with, making
    them very difficult to learn)

  * types of errors that get thrown under what conditions

  * description of what the function does

  * examples of how the function is used in practice

I don't really underestand R well enough to talk about the
types myself or error handling, other than in broad generalities.

You'll see that using primitive functions will make writing
this spec much easier, which will in turn make development and
testing much easier.  It should also make it easier to play around
with higher-level functions that may be more changeable and less
well supported (due to prohibitive combinatorics of testing and doc).

- Bob

You're right.  Part of this spec should be choosing good names.

I think we should step back and rename a bunch of functions and deprecate

"optimizing" or nouns like "stan_model");  I'd also prefer class names
to be nouns ("stanmodel" is good).  But if R uses gerunds for functions,

users won't either, but maybe we just need to tell them (and me)
to go learn R.

I think this means I should just butt out of R design.
I'd like the doc to be something I can understand, but I realize
I may just be too clueless about R to qualify as an RStan user.

That's great!   (The earthly idea, though not my intention,
for duplicated function names is discoverability.  I didn't think
save() and load() worked for Rcpp objects --- didn't we have a long
discussion about why it's nearly impossible to serialize?  Isn't that
why we read the data back into R data structures?  Or did things change?

So it sounds like we pretty much have everything that I want
in terms of functionality.

Are the other functions like stan() built on top of these,
or implemented independently?

Linguistic aside: most nouns can be verbed.  And the "-ing"
forms are a mess, because they act as present participle verbs
and gerundive nouns (e.g., "John was running" vs. "The running of
the race").  So it's definitely not clear cut.

Then there are constructors, which are function-like but
usually named after nouns.

Anyway, it's not a very strong convention anywhere.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] if else confusion
messages.body_plain:
On Jun 7, 2014, at 6:04 PM, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:

> No matter how I try to specialize OperandsAndPartials, I always get an error similar to whats below. Does this mean that in order for this to work we'd have to have 5*2 different implementations (for OperandsAndPartials with just T1,T2 and then just T1,T2,T3... etc.)?

No.  You should be able to get away with one that is
sufficiently polymorphic, the same way it is currently
done for double and var implementations.

The trick is that all the functions/operations you apply
in the body of a template need to be grammatically well
formed for all possible type instantiations.

One way to do this is with conditionals based on traits
(properties of types) and dummy overloads.  Anotehr is by
using expression templates.

I'd suggest you start diving into the Josuttis and Vandevoorde
templates book --- I think there's a copy in the office, or you might
be able to get it online through the Columbia library.

- Bob

> I can't seem to find much about using boost::enable_if with structs. And I'm not sure how I would use the disable_if as you suggested unless you mean something like
>
> template<typename T1=boost::disable_if_c<contains_fvar<T1,T2,T3,T4,T5,T6>::value,double>::type,

> You may need to use something like Boost's enable_if to
> make sure you don't wind up with multiple instantiations.
> You have to make sure that there's a unique most-specific
> match.
>
> So you can't have:
>
>   template <typename T> foo(T x, double y);
>   template <typename T> foo(double x, T y);
>
> and try to call
>
>   foo(double,double)
>
> because both the declarations match equally well.
>
> But then you can use something like disable_if to ensure
> that T in one of the cases is never instantiated if T
> is a double.

messages.body_plain:
On Jun 7, 2014, at 6:04 PM, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:

> No matter how I try to specialize OperandsAndPartials, I always get an error similar to whats below. Does this mean that in order for this to work we'd have to have 5*2 different implementations (for OperandsAndPartials with just T1,T2 and then just T1,T2,T3... etc.)?

No.  You should be able to get away with one that is
sufficiently polymorphic, the same way it is currently
done for double and var implementations.

The trick is that all the functions/operations you apply
in the body of a template need to be grammatically well
formed for all possible type instantiations.

One way to do this is with conditionals based on traits
(properties of types) and dummy overloads.  Anotehr is by
using expression templates.

I'd suggest you start diving into the Josuttis and Vandevoorde
templates book --- I think there's a copy in the office, or you might
be able to get it online through the Columbia library.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, June 10, 2014 9:51:18 PM UTC-4, Peter Li wrote:
> Thoughts

This does not really respond to Peter's question, but I think the current distribution tests are overkill. They take forever and don't catch bugs very efficiently.

Currently, we are testing all combinations var and double (possibly in vectors) for all of the arguments, and I guess soon for the various fvar types. I think we could get away with just testing that each distribution works when all of its arguments are simultaneously of type T.

This would not catch bugs where, in the normal distribution example, y is a double vector, mu is a var vector, and sigma is a double, etc. But all those combinations are really just exercising the type promotion stuff, which is something that could be (and hopefully is) done more directly with unit tests. And I think after this release comes out, we should switch to C++11 and be using auto internally inside the distributions, so that the scope for such bugs is a lot narrower.

Maybe it is worthwhile to make sure the compiler is instantiating all the various combinations of arguments correctly, but that could be done much more quickly by putting those in the -fsyntax-only pile.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Distribution Testing
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jun 11, 2014 at 11:47 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> This does not really respond to Peter's question, but I think the current distribution tests are overkill. They take forever and don't catch bugs very efficiently.

Sorry, Ben, but I'm not going to budge on testing our distributions.
1. They're not overkill. They're actually underkill. There are ways bugs can still get through.
2. They take a long time, but it isn't forever. If you're talking about catching gradient bugs inefficiently, I've had to hunt down bugs in gradients of our distributions by creating a model, running it, comparing the model distribution to what we expect it to be, figuring out which distributions it calls, finding out the parameter values that get passed into each distribution, making sure those all work, just to identify which piece has a bug. To me, that's much more inefficient. By the way, to test a single distribution family, including all the compilation time, it takes under 2 mins. I tested the normal distribution.
3. It may be overkill to run it on each commit, although I don't think so. Unfortunately, testing traits and other templated code might have weird effects that we can't effectively "unit" test. Or fail to somehow. That really means we should be testing it somewhere else, but they're things that we're not even aware we should be testing.
4. These tests have been really effective in stopping defective vectorized distributions. I don't think you, Ben, have written any, so I'm not sure you're aware of the complexity of the way we're writing the distributions now. When we used to use auto-diff directly, even over vector arguments, life was a lot easier and we really didn't need this type of testing. Now, with all the optimizations we've taken with the distributions, these test make it a lot easier and quicker to get out more correct code.

I'm not saying that this is the best way to do it. If you can come up with something better, please, implement it or let someone know.

>
> Currently, we are testing all combinations var and double (possibly in vectors) for all of the arguments, and I guess soon for the various fvar types. I think we could get away with just testing that each distribution works when all of its arguments are simultaneously of type T.

Yes, we're testing every combination of var, double x scalar, vector, row_vector, array. We can't get away with just a single type of T. More below.

>
> This would not catch bugs where, in the normal distribution example, y is a double vector, mu is a var vector, and sigma is a double, etc. But all those combinations are really just exercising the type promotion stuff, which is something that could be (and hopefully is) done more directly with unit tests. And I think after this release comes out, we should switch to C++11 and be using auto internally inside the distributions, so that the scope for such bugs is a lot narrower.

So, this is where you're missing the point of this testing. It isn't exercising the type promotion. We're actually doing things at the double level, for these distributions.

Suppose there's a 2 argument probability distribution. If the first is scalar and the second is scalar, that's easy. If they're both vectors, that's easy too. The gradients are as expected. If the first is scalar and the second is a vector, the expression graph is going to put the first on the expression graph multiple times and the derivative with respect to that first variable is going to have to be adjusted. Same with the second variable.

We've "caught" a lot of bugs using the framework. It's really easy, as a programmer, to get indexes mixed up and increment the wrong derivative. It's easy to forget to loop over both variables in the same way. It's easy to forget to compute a vector of things if you needed them. These things should be straight-forward, and were at one point before we started optimizing our distribution code. To do what we're doing, I'd argue we need something like our current framework or better.

> Maybe it is worthwhile to make sure the compiler is instantiating all the various combinations of arguments correctly, but that could be done much more quickly by putting those in the -fsyntax-only pile.
>
> Ben
>
>

Sorry, but I'm adamant about keeping this level of testing as a minimum for the distribution tests. If you know of a faster way to do it, please let us know. Just FYI, we test:
- all versions of the function are callable (this is the instantiation that you're talking about)
- values, specified by the test writer, are callable
- invalid values, specified by the test writer, throw exceptions
- make sure the proportionality constant is actually constant
- we test against finite diff, just in case we messed up our hand calculations
- we test against a second implementation, usually pure auto-diff, specified in the test itself
- we test with each value repeated in a vector. We make sure the log prob value is a multiple of the first, we make sure the gradient value is a multiple when it's a scalar and the other arguments have been broadcast.
- we test with a 0 length vector

I think it's an ugly testing framework, but does the job, for now. I'd be happy to replace it.

(row)vector of double, (row)vector of double, ...
(row)vector of var, (row)vector of var, ...
(row)vector of fvar<double>, (row)vector of fvar<double>, ...
(row)vector of fvar<var>, (row)vector of fvar<var>, ...

> 1. They're not overkill. They're actually underkill. There are ways bugs can still get through.
> 2. They take a long time, but it isn't forever. If you're talking about catching gradient bugs inefficiently, I've had to hunt down bugs in gradients of our distributions by creating a model, running it, comparing the model distribution to what we expect it to be, figuring out which distributions it calls, finding out the parameter values that get passed into each distribution, making sure those all work, just to identify which piece has a bug. To me, that's much more inefficient. By the way, to test a single distribution family, including all the compilation time, it takes under 2 mins. I tested the normal distribution.

The normal is not so bad because it only has 3 arguments; exp_mod_normal and stuff are a lot worse. And these tests are a pretty big barrier for implementing distributions with 5 or 6 arguments where MCMC or MML should have a big advantage over ML. But in the plain normal case, what sort of gradient bug would be caught by testing {double, double, var}, {double, var, double}, {double, var, var}, {var, double, double}, {var, var, double}, {var, double, var}, that wouldn't be caught just by testing {var, var, var}?

> 3. It may be overkill to run it on each commit, although I don't think so. Unfortunately, testing traits and other templated code might have weird effects that we can't effectively "unit" test. Or fail to somehow. That really means we should be testing it somewhere else, but they're things that we're not even aware we should be testing.

I think that implies we're doing it wrong.

> 4. These tests have been really effective in stopping defective vectorized distributions. I don't think you, Ben, have written any, so I'm not sure you're aware of the complexity of the way we're writing the distributions now. When we used to use auto-diff directly, even over vector arguments, life was a lot easier and we really didn't need this type of testing. Now, with all the optimizations we've taken with the distributions, these test make it a lot easier and quicker to get out more correct code.
>
> I'm not saying that this is the best way to do it. If you can come up with something better, please, implement it or let someone know.

See the end, but also to replace as much of the type promotion stuff as possible with auto and decltype.

> >
> > Currently, we are testing all combinations var and double (possibly in vectors) for all of the arguments, and I guess soon for the various fvar types. I think we could get away with just testing that each distribution works when all of its arguments are simultaneously of type T.
>
> Yes, we're testing every combination of var, double x scalar, vector, row_vector, array. We can't get away with just a single type of T. More below.
>
>
> >
> > This would not catch bugs where, in the normal distribution example, y is a double vector, mu is a var vector, and sigma is a double, etc. But all those combinations are really just exercising the type promotion stuff, which is something that could be (and hopefully is) done more directly with unit tests. And I think after this release comes out, we should switch to C++11 and be using auto internally inside the distributions, so that the scope for such bugs is a lot narrower.
>
> So, this is where you're missing the point of this testing. It isn't exercising the type promotion. We're actually doing things at the double level, for these distributions.
>
> Suppose there's a 2 argument probability distribution. If the first is scalar and the second is scalar, that's easy. If they're both vectors, that's easy too. The gradients are as expected. If the first is scalar and the second is a vector, the expression graph is going to put the first on the expression graph multiple times and the derivative with respect to that first variable is going to have to be adjusted. Same with the second variable.

I get that. To me, that is an area where we should (if we don't already) have unit-tests of the OperandsAndPartials and ScalarTypeVectorView and whatnot. We definitely need to make sure that the expression graph has the right number of leaves and stuff for all possible inputs. But given that, I don't see why we need to re-verify that for all distributions that utilize OperandsAndPartials and ScalarTypeVectorView because the structure of the expression graph doesn't depend on the particularities of the partial derivatives.

> We've "caught" a lot of bugs using the framework. It's really easy, as a programmer, to get indexes mixed up and increment the wrong derivative. It's easy to forget to loop over both variables in the same way. It's easy to forget to compute a vector of things if you needed them. These things should be straight-forward, and were at one point before we started optimizing our distribution code. To do what we're doing, I'd argue we need something like our current framework or better.

It seems to me that off-by-one and other indexing errors would be caught with a homogenous test of {vector<var>, vector<var>, ...}.

> Sorry, but I'm adamant about keeping this level of testing as a minimum for the distribution tests. If you know of a faster way to do it, please let us know. Just FYI, we test:
> - all versions of the function are callable (this is the instantiation that you're talking about)

okay, that part is amenable to -fsyntax-only

> - values, specified by the test writer, are callable

not sure what you mean by that

> - invalid values, specified by the test writer, throw exceptions

if the invalid value throws an exception for homogenous invalid argument types, then it should throw an exception for mixed invalid argument types

> - make sure the proportionality constant is actually constant

I think this could be verified with homogenous double argument types.

> - we test against finite diff, just in case we messed up our hand calculations
> - we test against a second implementation, usually pure auto-diff, specified in the test itself

I think these could be verified with all homogenous not-double argument types, like {var, var, ...}, {vector<var>, vector<var>, ...}, {fvar<double>, fvar<double>, ...}, etc.

> - we test with each value repeated in a vector. We make sure the log prob value is a multiple of the first, we make sure the gradient value is a multiple when it's a scalar and the other arguments have been broadcast.

If I am understanding you correctly, I think that could be a unit-test rather than a bunch of distribution-specific tests. In other words, whether we get that right doesn't have to do with what value the partial derivative takes.

> - we test with a 0 length vector

Just need a homogenous call with {vector<double>, vector<double>, ...} where the vectors are each length zero. We don't need to also do {vector<var>, vector<var>, ...} there.

Ben

That's the crux of the matter.  If you look at the code, template
traits are used to select branches in the code based on whether the
argument is a var or a double.  If it's double, you drop the term.

Doing what wrong?

Not quite, because there are different branches in the code
in many cases.  The point that Ben's made before and I'll second
is that we want to test coverage.  But it's not just coverage,

This has saved us on many occasions.

messages.body_plain:
If model is a string then it just has to compile it afresh each time.  But indeed we should be discouraging this (in particular, we should not have an “model in a string” examples in the Rstan quick start guide).

On Jun 12, 2014, at 1:30 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> That's still not quite precise enough to be a spec.
>
> I take it by make-like behavior here, you want to recompile
> if the time stamp of the model file is later than that of
> the compiled version.
>
> But what do you do if the model's given as a string, which
> seems to be popular among our R users.  Personally, I'd try
> to discourage that behavior because it's a pain for us
> to debug when everything's tied up in R --- I believe most of our
> C++ developers don't ever use R.  But then I don't like
> Sweave (or whatever it's called now) for the same reason.
>
> Andrew --- could you go through ALL the other arguments
> to stan() and make sure they're what you want?
>
> I would very much like to avoid continually changing our
> functions.  Let's try to get it as close to right in a single
> change.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jun 11, 2014, at 5:36 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>

>> Hi--I think it's fine to have various primitive functions as long as the wrappers do what I need.  I need a stan() function that has what Bob calls make-like behavior and is set by default to save the compiled models in the working directory, similarly a stan_optimize() function (or some other name) that does the same thing with optimization and returns an object from which we can extract the mode, the second-derivative matrix, and various other things.  Also we need various verbose options including complete silence as an option.  It's fine with me if this is all done by calling the basic functions; indeed, I think this will make the documentation that much clearer.

>> A
>>
>> On Jun 7, 2014, at 12:14 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>>> On Jun 6, 2014, at 9:53 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>
>>>> Hi, Bob.  I put it on stan-dev because non R-users might have thoughts too.
>>>
>>> Thanks.
>>>
>>>> At some point we can talk about how best to write a spec.  My main thought is to switch to Sebastian's function (or something like it), also to clean up the stan-optimize call and a few other things.
>>>
>>> I don't think we need a formal spec process --- just
>>> a simple functional spec consisting of the documentation for
>>> the functions you want to see implemented including examples.
>>> Then, the folks who know R can turn it into a technical spec
>>> that explains how to implement it, but I don't think we
>>> need to formalize a technical spec if the functional spec is solid.
>>>
>>> I'll go first with a really informal functional spec just consisting
>>> of examples.  Here's what I would like to see for compilation:
>>>
>>> model <- compile("foo.stan");
>>>
>>> for fitting:
>>>
>>> mle_fit <- optimize(model=, data=, ...);
>>> mcmc_fit <- stan(model=, data=, ...);
>>>
>>> and for saving and reloading:
>>>
>>> save_model(model=, file=);
>>> model <- load_model(file=);
>>>
>>> To turn this into a functional spec we can work from,
>>> we have to add descriptions of
>>>
>>> * the rest of the arguments
>>>
>>> * types for each argument
>>>
>>> * return type
>>>
>>> * constraints on legal calling patterns --- the spec has to
>>>   say exactly what arguments require other arguments or disallow
>>>   other arguments, and what sets of legal values there are (this
>>>   is the killer that most R functions don't even bother with, making
>>>   them very difficult to learn)
>>>
>>> * types of errors that get thrown under what conditions
>>>
>>> * description of what the function does
>>>
>>> * examples of how the function is used in practice
>>>
>>> I don't really underestand R well enough to talk about the
>>> types myself or error handling, other than in broad generalities.
>>>
>>> You'll see that using primitive functions will make writing
>>> this spec much easier, which will in turn make development and
>>> testing much easier.  It should also make it easier to play around
>>> with higher-level functions that may be more changeable and less
>>> well supported (due to prohibitive combinatorics of testing and doc).
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>> A
>>>>
>>>> On Jun 5, 2014, at 10:24 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> 1.  Do you have a spec for how you think it should be
>>>>> rewritten to be less clunky?
>>>>>
>>>>> 2.  Should we move this discussion to stan-dev, or perhaps
>>>>> start an rstan-dev mailing list?
>>>>>
>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>
>>>>> On Jun 5, 2014, at 1:20 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>>> Hi all.  Maybe next week when we've finished this current grant application, we can talk about fixing up Rstan.  Right now, running stan from R is clunky, and doing mle requires a ton of function calls.  So I'd like to put some new functions in Rstan (and clean up the functions we have) so this can all be done.  Thx
>>>>>> A
>>>>>>
>>>>>> On May 23, 2014, at 6:58 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>
>>>>>>> OK, 2 functions is fine.  Maybe stan() and stan_optimize()?  Or optimize_stan()?  What do you think?
>>>>>>> A
>>>>>>> On May 23, 2014, at 6:35 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> On May 23, 2014, at 4:09 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> Hi all.  What's most important to me is that the workhorse stan() function have make-like behavior.  I _don't_ want to have to call stan() one way the first time (passing it the file name) and another way a later time (passing it the R object name).
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> Perhaps given what you two say, we should have the three primitive functions as you define them, and then have one or more wrappers of the sort that I like.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> That would make me happier.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> The wrappers would include the following:
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> - stan() with make-like behavior
>>>>>>>>> - the same thing for stan_optimize (or maybe that should just be stan() with optimize=TRUE; I don't feel strongly about this)
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> I feel pretty strongly that these should not be merged
>>>>>>>> into a single command.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Optimization and sampling take different parameters and
>>>>>>>> produce different output data structures.  Combining them
>>>>>>>> then becomes this big conditional exercise.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Compare:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> c foo(a,b)
>>>>>>>> d bar(e,f);
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> with
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> [c OR d] foo_bar(a, b, e, f);
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> + doc that if a or b is defined then return is c and
>>>>>>>> e and f can't be and vice-versa
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Let's not be foo_bar!
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Distribution Testing
messages.body_plain:
I just wanted to mention, the runtime of the tests is very short. It's almost all in compilation time.

Just timing on my machine: total time to compile and run the normal distribution tests (24 of them), as reported by time:
real    1m49.751s
user    9m34.293s
sys    0m26.228s

The runtime (recorded by google test)
 1.681s

So, it's really not the runtime of the tests that matter. We need to get a faster build.

On Thu, Jun 12, 2014 at 7:42 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
> On Jun 11, 2014, at 8:24 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > But in the plain normal case, what sort of gradient bug would be caught by testing {double, double, var}, {double, var, double}, {double, var, var}, {var, double, double}, {var, var, double}, {var, double, var}, that wouldn't be caught just by testing {var, var, var}?
>
> That's the crux of the matter.  If you look at the code, template
> traits are used to select branches in the code based on whether the
> argument is a var or a double.  If it's double, you drop the term.
>
> Also, the vector vs. var invokes all the expression template view machinery.
>
> >
> > 3. It may be overkill to run it on each commit, although I don't think so. Unfortunately, testing traits and other templated code might have weird effects that we can't effectively "unit" test. Or fail to somehow. That really means we should be testing it somewhere else, but they're things that we're not even aware we should be testing.
> >
> > I think that implies we're doing it wrong.
>
> Doing what wrong?
>
> > It seems to me that off-by-one and other indexing errors would be caught with a homogenous test of {vector<var>, vector<var>, ...}.
>
> Not quite, because there are different branches in the code
> in many cases.  The point that Ben's made before and I'll second
> is that we want to test coverage.  But it's not just coverage,
> it's the combinatorics of how the evaluations can go.
>
> Like Daniel, I can't see any way of getting around this.
>
> > - invalid values, specified by the test writer, throw exceptions
> >
> > if the invalid value throws an exception for homogenous invalid argument types, then it should throw an exception for mixed invalid argument types
>
> I think that's right.
>
> > - make sure the proportionality constant is actually constant
> >
> > I think this could be verified with homogenous double argument types.
>
> Not quite --- see above.
>
> > - we test against finite diff, just in case we messed up our hand calculations
>
> This has saved us on many occasions.
>
> > - we test against a second implementation, usually pure auto-diff, specified in the test itself
>
> I'm not sure we need both of these.
>
> > - we test with each value repeated in a vector. We make sure the log prob value is a multiple of the first, we make sure the gradient value is a multiple when it's a scalar and the other arguments have been broadcast.
> >
> > If I am understanding you correctly, I think that could be a unit-test rather than a bunch of distribution-specific tests. In other words, whether we get that right doesn't have to do with what value the partial derivative takes.
>
> I don't quite understand what you're suggesting here.
>
> - Bob

The only issue I see is that the tests in autodiff are not vectorized. That's not an issue except for when we do test_repeat_as_vector() when parameters are repeated as vectors and then passed in. Also, it seems like you can't have a function and use inputs something like double double fvar<double>.

I'm also confused at how I would use the stuff in autodiff.hpp to calculate higher order derivatives (namely second and third) since they don't use the var call .grad at all. [If you want to see what I'm referring to look in the branch at test_fixture_distr.hpp]

Let me know if there are any workarounds for these. In any case, I think the way I've got most of testing implemented now, even if we change the autodiff system, it would only change types and the small functions where we compute derivatives like

  double calculate_gradients_3rdorder(vector<double>& grad,
                                      fvar<fvar<var> >& logprob,
                                      vector<var>& x) {
    logprob.d_.d_.grad(x, grad);
    return logprob.val_.val_.val();
  }

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Distribution Testing
messages.body_plain:
I've added higher order finite-diff tests, but the issue is that when the types are something like fvar<var>,fvar<var>,double, the derivative of logp will be something like (dlogp/dx1) *dx1_ + (dlogp/dx2)*dx2_, so then when we take the gradient of this, what we get isn't actually the partial derivatives d^2/dx1^2 and d^2/dx2^2. Instead, it's a combination of what we want and d^2/dx1dx2.

In any case, it might be difficult to test this, but first order always works and I think since calculating higher order partial derivatives just reuses the first order code, we might be ok since the individual functions have higher order partial derivative tests (which I'm still working on adding for some matrix operations).

On Thu, Jun 12, 2014 at 1:18 PM, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> This particular one is for fvar<fvar<var> > types. x is the vector of all the vars that we are taking the gradient to. So for all the parameters that are of type fvar<fvar<var> > i added param[i].val_.val_ to the vector x. And then we're taking the gradient of logprob with respect to these vars to get the resulting vector grad which will consist of doubles. I defined functions like these for all the types. I think that with the new autodiff, most of what we need to change should be mostly only these functions.
>
>
> On Thu, Jun 12, 2014 at 12:39 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Jun 12, 2014, at 5:18 PM, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > The only issue I see is that the tests in autodiff are not vectorized. That's not an issue except for when we do test_repeat_as_vector() when parameters are repeated as vectors and then passed in. Also, it seems like you can't have a function and use inputs something like double double fvar<double>.
> >
> > You need to define the appropriate functor.  It may not
> > be worth doing.
> >
> > > I'm also confused at how I would use the stuff in autodiff.hpp to calculate higher order derivatives (namely second and third) since they don't use the var call .grad at all. [If you want to see what I'm referring to look in the branch at test_fixture_distr.hpp]
> >
> > There's a Hessian function for 2nd order and you can add a 3rd order
> > version to autodiff.hpp.
> >
> > > Let me know if there are any workarounds for these. In any case, I think the way I've got most of testing implemented now, even if we change the autodiff system, it would only change types and the small functions where we compute derivatives like
> > >
> > >   double calculate_gradients_3rdorder(vector<double>& grad,
> > >                                       fvar<fvar<var> >& logprob,
> > >                                       vector<var>& x) {
> > >     logprob.d_.d_.grad(x, grad);
> > >     return logprob.val_.val_.val();
> > >   }
> >
> > I'm not following the types here. First of all, where's the function
> > that's being evaluated?
> >
> > In general, I think we ONLY need to define and test inputs where
> > every type is either the highest type or double/int.  We won't
> > be calling things like normal_log(fvar<var>, var, double)
> > or anything like that.
> >
> > - Bob

messages.subject: 2.4+ manual and ease of finding things
messages.subject_clean: 2.4+ manual and ease of finding things
messages.body_plain:
The 2.3 manual isn't going to make things easier to find.

In fact, it splits out the CmdStan part, which will arguably
make things harder to find.

Michael drafted a new manual outline that'll hopefully make
things easier.  Andrew and I have also been discussing some re-orgs.

But this particular issue, support matching constraints, is
emphasized right up front in the CmdStan manual.

The hard-to-find problem is intrinsic to large systems because
you can't emphasize everything.  We could add an index,
but I don't think it'll help with this kind of thing, because
it's an unknown unknown for a user and they won't know what
to look up.

- Bob

>>>
>>> For distributions like the GEV where the support depends on the parameter values, you have to be clever with the declarations in the parameters section. Otherwise, you get into a situation where what Stan thinks are valid parameter values have zero or undefined density values. In your case, it would be something like
>>>
>>> data {
>>>   int<lower=0> n;   vector[n] t;   real y[n];}
>>> transformed data {
>>>   real min_y;
>>>   real max_y;
>>>   min_y <- min(y);
>>>   max_y <- max(y);
>>> }
>>> parameters {
>>>   real xi;
>>>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>>>   real<lower=if_else( xi > 0, min_y + sigma / xi, negative_infinity() ),
>>>        upper=if_else( xi > 0, infinity(), max_y + sigma / xi )> mu;
>>> }
>>> model {
>>>   real z;
>>>   for(i in 1:n) {
>>>     z <- 1 + (y[i] - mu) * xi / sigma;
>>>     increment_log_prob(-log(sigma) - (1 + 1/xi)*log(z[n]) - pow(z,-1/xi));
>>>   }
>>>   // priors on xi, sigma, and mu
>>> }

messages.body_plain:
v2.3.0 (16 June 2014)
======================================================================
Bug Fixes
------------
* fixed poisson_rng, neg_binomial_rng
* integer overflow now throws errors
* allow < and > within range constraints
* support MS Visual Studio 2008
* fixed bug in lkj

Features
------------
* functions added to Stan language!
* turned off eigen asserts
* CmdStan is now in its own repository
* added quad_form_sym, multi_gp_log, multi_gp,
  multi_normal_cholesky_rng, to_matrix, to_vector, to_array, flatten,
  qr_Q, qr_R
* added JSON parser to Stan
* a^b syntax for pow(a,b)

On Monday, June 16, 2014 5:44:37 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Is there a design everyone agrees on somewhere for which new functions
> you want?  Is it just changes to existing functions (for what I've been
> calling "make-like" and you've been calling "Sebastian's function(s?)").

No. But more than that, not everyone thinks it is a good idea.

I think I'm outvoted, but I will just say it one more time: If stan() were to automatically save the stanfit object to foo.RData, then it would be in violation of CRAN's policy against malicious behavior

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/policies.html

which states "The code and examples provided in a package should never do anything which might be regarded as malicious or anti-social. The following are illustrative examples from past experience ... Packages should not write in the users' home filespace, nor anywhere else on the file system apart from the R session's temporary directory". If packages were to do that, it would be easy for users to unwittingly overwrite results that they explicitly saved to the disk.

So, if we do this, rstan will never be able to go onto CRAN. I think the lack of binary installation via the usual mechanism from CRAN is a problem that is two or three orders of magnitude worse than the problem that people who do not know enough R to save() and load() their own stuff have to wait an extra minute while it compiles in the relatively rare case that they want to run the same model in different R sessions.

We could implement the autoloading behavior without the autosaving behavior, although I don't know if that would justify delaying the release. Whatever we decide to do, we should do it now because we have the Meetup downtown next Tuesday with about 25 people signed up to learn how to install various flavors of Stan.

Ben

P.S.  One intermediate step we could take, while still arguing about the rest, is to standardize default names.

For example, suppose we run the following function call:
object <- stan(foo.stan,…)
or
object <- stan_optimize(foo.stan,…)

The function can handle this as follows by first looking for a file “foo.stan” in the working directory and an object “foo.stan” in the workspace,  Then:
1.  If the object foo.stan in the working directory exists and has been updated more recently than the foo.stan file (or if there is no foo.stan file), then Stan will just use the foo.stan object as the compiled model and run it.
2.  If the object foo.stan in the working directory exists but the file foo.stan has been updated more recently, then Stan will recompile the model from the file and overwrite it as foo.stan in the working directory, then run it.
3.  If there is no object foo.stan in the working directory but the file foo.stan exists, then Stan will compile the model from the file, save the compiled model as foo.stan, and run it.
4.  If there is no object foo.stan in the working directory and no file foo.stan, then Stan will spit out an error.

The above can be default behavior.  We can have an option that saves into the directory also.

But it’s important for me to have some of this functionality.  As it is, my code is a mess.  Running things with 0 chains, etc., it’s horrible.  When people use Bugs/Jags, they have to do hack after hack.  I don’t want Stan users to be hacking in this way.

Also, we need some verbose options.
A

messages.subject: Andrew's RStan feature requests
messages.body_plain:
Andrew --- for me, the problem isn't that I'm arguing you
shouldn't get these functions, but that I don't quite understand
what you're asking for.  I want to create a functional spec
so there's no misunderstandings.  This is why people write specs!

We'll have to update it via e-mail because Andrew doesn't want
to use the Wiki.   Andrew --- if you want to make changes, can you
just edit what's below and re-send, rather than just sending comments?
That way, we'll at least have one coherent spec we're all working from.

I'm meeting Andrew on Thursday and hopefully we can go over this
and flesh it out into something that an R developer can comment on
and then generate a technical spec, implementation, doc, and tests for.
If anything below is impossible or bad behavior, please let me know before
then.

ANDREW'S FEATURE REQUESTS
========================================================

1.  stan_optimize() and stan_sample()
--------------------------------------------------------

1.a.  Add a function stan_optimize() that behaves like
stan() in terms of specifying the model (more on that below).

1.b.  Deprecate the function optimizing() by printing a warning
to the user.

1.c.  Add a function stan_sample() to replace stan().

1.d.  Deprecate the stan() function.

2.  Make-like behavior (aka "Sebastian's function")
--------------------------------------------------------

When stan_optimize() or stan() are passed a model file, try
the following in order

2.a. check to see if a compiled version of the model exists in
     memory that is newer than the model file time stamp, and if so, use that

2.b. check to see if a compiled version of the model exists on the
     file system that's newer than the model file time stamp, and if so,
     use that

2.c. compile the model and save it in memory, then
     if the user has specified a save-file argument, save a version
     of the model to that file which can be read in later;  suggest
     users choose an appropriate suffix based on R conventions.

QUESTION:  Do we add any similar functionality for models passed as strings?

3.  Verbosity options
------------------------------------------------------
a quiet option that turns off all output.

======================================================

GENERAL QUESTION:  Andrew wanted us to standardize names, but I don't see
any suggestions as to what to use and I don't understand which names we're
talking about.

COMMENT:  I would very much like to have a binary CRAN install.  I'm
tired of all the failed install traffic on the mailing list.  Not
that I'm very optimistic given R's gatekeepers.

Some further comments below, mainly for Andrew.

On Jun 17, 2014, at 5:52 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> P.S.  One intermediate step we could take, while still arguing about the rest, is to standardize default names.

I don't think anyone's arguing here.  If there's a spec
we can agree on, then I think any of this behavior will be
easy to build on the primitives.

I think the main issue is figuring out exactly what
you (Andrew) want in terms of functionality and then
figuring out how to do it in a way that's idiomatic
and cross platform and not considered antagonistic by the
R community.

> For example, suppose we run the following function call:

> object <- stan(foo.stan,…)
> or
> object <- stan_optimize(foo.stan,…)

Those are going to need quotes around "foo.stan", right?
One thing that always confuses me in R is where you need
quotes and where you don't.  Why in the world does it accept
library(rstan) and not insist on library('rstan')?  No idea,
but then that's why I'm not designing the R interface, just trying
to extract your (Andrew's) functional requirements.

> The function can handle this as follows by first looking for a file “foo.stan” in the working directory and an object “foo.stan” in the workspace,

What's the workspace?  You mean in memory?  And if so,
shouldn't we check memory, then file system, then recompile
in that order?  That's what I suggested above.

> Then:

> 1.  If the object foo.stan in the working directory exists and has been updated more recently than the foo.stan file (or if there is no foo.stan file), then Stan will just use the foo.stan object as the compiled model and run it.

??? I think you're using "foo.stan" for two different
things here --- the text of the model file and the serialized
(saved to disk) version of the compiled model.  Can we at
least give the saved file a different name that follows R
serialization conventions?

> 2.  If the object foo.stan in the working directory exists but the file foo.stan has been updated more recently, then Stan will recompile the model from the file and overwrite it as foo.stan in the working directory, then run it.
> 3.  If there is no object foo.stan in the working directory but the file foo.stan exists, then Stan will compile the model from the file, save the compiled model as foo.stan, and run it.
> 4.  If there is no object foo.stan in the working directory and no file foo.stan, then Stan will spit out an error.

Writing into the working directory is the behavior that
R considers anti-social.

> The above can be default behavior.  We can have an option that saves into the directory also.

Saves into what directory?  Did my reformulation above capture
what you're after?

>
> But it’s important for me to have some of this functionality.

I'm not sure what the full scope of "this functionality" is.  Just
what you listed above?

> As it is, my code is a mess.  Running things with 0 chains, etc.,

Why are you running things with 0 chains?  There's a model
compile function.  Did I miss something?

> it’s horrible.

What else specifically do you find horrible?  And how would
you rather see it behave?

> When people use Bugs/Jags, they have to do hack after hack.  I don’t want Stan users to be hacking in this way.
>
> Also, we need some verbose options.

I listed the full quiet mode.  Is there other verbosity levels
you're after?  If so, how should they behave?

- Bob

      something.  The commit log's pretty long since 2.2, which
      was mid-February.

v.2.3.0 (18 June 2014)
======================================================================

We had a record number of user-submitted patches for this release.
Thanks to everyone who helped out!

New Features
------------
* user-defined function definitions added to Stan language
* cholesky_corr data type for Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
* a^b syntax for pow(a,b)
* reshaping functions: to_matrix(), to_vector(), to_row_vector(),
  to_array_1d(), to_array_2d()
* matrix operations: quad_form_sym() (x' *Sigma * x), QR decompositions
  qr_Q(), qr_R()
* densities: Gaussian processes multi_gp_log(), multi_gp(),
  and alternative negative binomial parameterization neg_binomial_2()
* random number generator: multi_normal_cholesky_rng()
* sorting: sort_indices_*() for returning indexes sorted by value
* many fixes to I/O for data and inits to check consistency and
  report errors
* removed some uses of std::cout where they don't belong
* updated parser for C++11 compatibility (thanks to Rob Goedman)
* added JSON parser to C++ (not exposed through interfaces yet)

New Developer
--------------
* added Marco Inacio as core developer

Optimizations
-------------
* turned off Eigen asserts
* efficiency improvements to posterior analysis print

Documentation
-------------
* Clarified licensing policy for individual code contributions
* Huge numbers of fixes to the documentation, including many
  user-contributed patches (thanks!), fixes to parallelization in
  CmdStan, Windows install instructions, boundaries for Dirichlet and
  Beta, removed suggestion to use floor and ceiling as indices,
  vectorized many models, clarified that && doesn't short circuit,
  clarified von Mises normalization, updated censoring doc (thanks
  to Alexey Stukalov), negative binomial doc enhanced, new references,
  new discussion of hierarchical models referencing Betancourt and
  Girolami paper, (Avraham Aadler and T Malsburg contributed patches)

Bug Fixes
------------
* fixed bug in lkj density
* fixed bug in Jacobian for corr_matrix data type
* fix cholesky_cov_matrix test code to allow use as parameter
* fixed poisson_rng, neg_binomial_rng
* allow binary operations (e.g., < and >) within range constraints
* support MS Visual Studio 2008
* fixed memory leaks in categorical sampling statement, categorical_log
  function, and softmax functions
* removed many compiler warnings
* numerous bug fixes to arithmetic test code conditions and messages,
  including calls from
* fixed model crashes when no parameter specified
* fixed template name conflicts for some compiler bugs (thanks Kevin
  S. Van Horn)

Code Reorganizations & Updates
------------------------------
* CmdStan is now in its own repository on GitHub: stan-dev/cmdstan
* consolidate and simplify error handling across modules
* pulled functionality from CmdStan command class and PyStan and RStan
  into Stan C++
* const correctness for chains (thanks Kevin S. Van Horn)
* generalized some interfaces to allow std::vector as well as Eigen
  for compatibility
* generalize some I/O CSV writer capabilities
* optimization output text cleaned up
* integer overflow during I/O now raises informative error messages

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Andrew's RStan feature requests
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Ben.  I was thinking that stan_save() would have certain default behavior, so that the model foo.stan would be saved as foo.rda or whatever.  I wanted to make things as smooth as possible.  If we had the “save” argument in the stan() and stan_optimize() functions then that might work too, as then these could call the regular save() functions.  As I was saying, for me it is awkward to have big objects hanging around in the workspace. Indeed I’ve sometimes been told that it is good R practice to _not_ rely on things being in the workspace but instead to have scripts be self-contained.  As a user, I really would like to just use stan() and stan_optimize() without having to use a different stan_compile() function the first time a model is called.
A

> I am pretty sure CRAN would consider to be malicious any function that writes to a non-temporary directory without the user explicitly requesting so. Maybe a save = TRUE argument to stan() would be adequate, but the usual approach would be for users to call save() if they want to save something. What would a stan_save() function do that is different from the save() function that works for any object?
>
> Ben
>

> What's unstable?  Is it some kind of range thing where
> we can just fail if they're outside that range?
> Or is the usual numerical instability of auto-diffing

Both.  The functions themselves are poorly implemented power
series and derivatives would be even worse (wether the series
were diff’d by hand or the autodiff was used explicity).

> And if so, do you know how to do it
> better?  Presumably you (Michael) have some solution up your sleeve
> for the new autodiff at higher orders.

Don’t allow CDFs for higher-order methods?  The new autodiff
has exections for functions without higher-order partials implemented
for exactly this purpose.

The real problem is that stable numerical implementations of these
nasty functions is way beyond our expertise.  If I had a few months
I might be able to find the old references, learn all the tricks, and
then implement them for everything.  But I don’t.

messages.subject: specs for Rstan!
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  Following my conversation with Bob the other day, here are a first draft of specs for the next rstan.  Bob can connect me if I’ve garbled anything.
A

The logic will be to consider a sequence of files or objects:

foo.stan [Stan program:  a text file]
foo.so [compiled model:  a dynamic shared object that exists in the R workspace]
foo.rda [compiled model:  stored as a file in the working directory for R, or maybe in a library directory of compiled Stan models]
foo.instantiated [instantiated model:  I assume this is a dynamic shared object too, it is created by putting the data into the compiled model]
foo.adapt [adaptation information for 1 chain:  a stan object of some sort]
foo.fit.single [fitted model for 1 chains:  a stan object]
foo.fit.multiple [fitted model for multiple chains:  a stan object that includes the simulations, R-hat, and n_eff, and the scramble code]
foo.fit.mle [fitted point estimate with cov matrix, conf intervals, possibly simulations]

And now the functions (I’ve tried to follow Bob’s principles here and keep the number of arguments to a minimum):

First, the sequence of primitives that lead to a fitted stan model:

foo.so <- stan_compile(“foo.stan”, boost_lib, eigen_lib, verbosity)
foo.instantiated <- stan_instantiate(foo.so, data, verbosity)
foo.adapt <- stan_adapt(foo.instantiated, algorithm(sub_arguments), init, seed, chain_id, n_warmup, verbosity)
foo.fit.single <- stan_simulate(foo.instantiated, foo.adapt, algorithm(sub_arguments), parameters_to_save, init, seed, chain_id, n_iter, verbosity)
foo.fit.multiple <- stan_combine(list(foo.fit.single.1,foo.fit.single.2,…), seed, verbosity)

Next, the primitives that do other things:

point.estimate <- stan_optimize(foo.instantiated, algorithm(sub_arguments), init, seed, verbosity)
log.prob <- stan_logprob(foo.instantiated, parameters, format)
gradient <- stan_gradient(foo.instantiated, parameters, format)
hessian <- stan_hessian(foo.instantiated, parameters, format)
In the above 3 functions, the “format” argument tells whether these are on the original or transformed scale, also they could be supplied as a list of named parameters or as a vector with all of them strung together.
parameters_new <- stan_transform(foo.instantiated, parameters) to transform forward and back

Next, the make function:

stan_make (“foo.stan”, data, file_save)

messages.subject: Re: specs for Rstan!
messages.body_plain:
This looks mostly fine. We should put in on a wiki page. If we are going to break everything, we might as well do it all at once and call it version 3.0 for the next Stan release and implement it for PyStan too. But if we are going to break everything, then it is worth seriously considering changing to "reference class" semantics. In R, see

help("setRefClass", "methods")

this is more Pythonic and C++-like, so it would probably help keep the interfaces consistent-ish.

I don't really get the purpose of the distinction between the .so / .dll dynamic shared object and the instantiated dynamic shared object with data. We don't currently associate the data with anything really, and it would seem like a superfluous copy to me.

I would rather not put the parallelism stuff into interfaces like rstan. It is easy enough to do on any particular computer and almost impossible to do in the abstract across all platforms where rstan might be used. And it would be different in PyStan. Chain-level parallelism should be done in Stan itself, possibly ASAP.

I got rstan to build and run without copying lib/, and we are down to 14MB on disk inclusive of a lot of cruft. Basically, we only need to copy src/stan and src/models into an RStan package, and even then we should probably split into multiple packages.

Ben

There is no model object on the C++ side before the data.
The model class's constructor takes a data reader argument and
upon construction, an instance will have its data assigned
to member variables.  The omission of no-arg constructor is by design
here, because none of the functions implemented by models can
be evaluated before the data is read in.  On construction, the
data is read in and the constructed model is guaranteed to be well
formed and immutable (and hence thread safe modulo the thread safety
of autodiff).

One place we need a model instance is to compute a log probability
function --- that doesn't take data as an argument.  It could
if we were willing to load in the data each time, but it seems
more likely that someone would re-use the same model object with
data in multiple calls.

One place where we need the dynamically linked code is to read
in new data in a call to stan(...).

- Bob

I want to refactor the function:
>     template <class Model>
>     int command(int argc, const char* argv[])

It is currently 769 lines and RStan pretty much reimplements the whole thing to run most of the functions. (I haven't looked at Allen's code, but my guess is PyStan also reimplements all of it.)

One way to deal with this is to change the interface to something like:
>     template <class Model, class SampleRecorder, class DiagnosticRecorder,
>                      class MessageRecorder, class InterruptHandler, ...>
>     int command(std::vector<argument*> arguments)

Each interface would be responsible for implementing the additional template parameters including the recorders and the "..." (tbd).
This function would then run based on what's passed in as arguments. It would be on the interfaces to translate to this argument structure.
This would allow interface designers to focus on implementing the different recorders, handlers, etc. and translate from the interface to an argument structure. This should stay backwards compatible always, so interface implementers can be behind Stan without penalty and being forced to change interface code with every new version.

Michael, was the original intent of the argument structure to be used as configuration?
As it currently stands
- there are no tests
- not sure how easy it is to validate configurations

Turns out I do have a lot of thoughts on this.  More below.

On Jun 24, 2014, at 6:05 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> I want to refactor the function:

>     template <class Model>
>     int command(int argc, const char* argv[])
>
> It is currently 769 lines and RStan pretty much reimplements the whole thing to run most of the functions. (I haven't looked at Allen's code, but my guess is PyStan also reimplements all of it.)

That would be great.  I thought that was where you
were heading when you dove into R in the first place.

This is also why I think the design for the current R
interface proposal from Andrew and Ben is so important.
We're thinking a 3.0 version that breaks backward compatibility
but is much more consistent along all these fronts.

> One way to deal with this is to change the interface to something like:
>     template <class Model, class SampleRecorder, class DiagnosticRecorder,
>                      class MessageRecorder, class InterruptHandler, ...>
>     int command(std::vector<argument*> arguments)

How about something like this:

template <class Model,
          class SampleWriter,
          class DiagnosticWriter,
          class MessageWriter,
          class InterruptHandler, ...>

    int command(const CmdConfig& config,
                const Model& model,
                SampleWriter& sampleRecorder,
                ...);

The classes won't be enough unless they can all be constructued
based on the config.  And this way the caller won't need to
specify the template args.

I very much like the idea of there being a config object
that the interfaces just populate.  If the mapping can be
general, then that's even better.

The only reasonable pattern for something general and
nested for config is the following

Simple:  properties objects map string keys to values,
where a value is either a string or another property
object

Sequence Values:  Add sequence values

Numeric Values:  Add numeric values.

With sequence and numeric values, we basically get something that
could be coded as strings in JSON and would have a direct analogue
as an R list or Python dictionary.  Then we can share the doc, with
only the method of constructing the nested object changing.  It's
not super idiomatic for R, but I like it --- we're breaking the regular
command-line idioms for the commnad-line config.  I don't know about Python's
idioms.

Defaults and Inheritance:  Java's Properties class implementation maintains
a pointer to a parent properties class (which may be null).  Keys are
first looked up in the local implementation, but if the key doesn't exist,
the call is delegated to the parent class.  The whole thing can be flattened
for transport.

I'm not sure the best way to nest this in C++.  A general
approach would be to use the variant structures from Boost that
are used in the abstract syntax tree for the parser, which has
the same problem in that right-hand sides can be one of many
things and you want to act differently for each.

Consistency:  if we can manage purely compositional consistency,
that would be awesome.  doc, testing and maintenance problems arise
as soon as values or existence of one key can depend on another (e.g.,
model string or model file in current setup).

- Bob

> that would be awesome.  doc, testing and maintenance problems arise
> as soon as values or existence of one key can depend on another (e.g.,
> model string or model file in current setup).

>From the command line, I think the only place I recall that has this sort of inconsistency is the init argument which could take a string or 0.

Just cause it might not be clear, I'm not in favor redo-ing work. If we can get the current argument infrastructure easy enough to get right from other interfaces other than the command line, I'd be happy.
