On Tue, Jun 24, 2014 at 12:02 PM, Allen Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
> Hi Daniel and Bob,
>
> This looks fine from the Python side of things; Rcpp and Cython do pretty much
> the same thing.
>
> That said, I'd urge erring on side of simplicity and C idioms for maximum
> compatibility with (future) wrapping libraries. For example, using a struct or
> an enum rather than a class when it's possible seems like a good idea.
>
> Best,
>
> -a
>
> On 06/24, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > I want to refactor the function:
> >
> > >     template <class Model>
> > >     int command(int argc, const char* argv[])
> > >
> >
> > It is currently 769 lines and RStan pretty much reimplements the whole
> > thing to run most of the functions. (I haven't looked at Allen's code, but
> > my guess is PyStan also reimplements all of it.)
> >
> >
> > One way to deal with this is to change the interface to something like:
> >
> > >     template <class Model, class SampleRecorder, class DiagnosticRecorder,
> > >                      class MessageRecorder, class InterruptHandler, ...>
> > >     int command(std::vector<argument*> arguments)
> > >
> >
> > Each interface would be responsible for implementing the additional
> > template parameters including the recorders and the "..." (tbd).
> > This function would then run based on what's passed in as arguments. It
> > would be on the interfaces to translate to this argument structure.
> > This would allow interface designers to focus on implementing the different
> > recorders, handlers, etc. and translate from the interface to an argument
> > structure. This should stay backwards compatible always, so interface
> > implementers can be behind Stan without penalty and being forced to change
> > interface code with every new version.
> >
> >
> > Michael, was the original intent of the argument structure to be used as
> > configuration?
> > As it currently stands
> > - there are no tests
> > - not sure how easy it is to validate configurations
> > - how would we handle changes to configuration over time?
> > - what helper methods are available for constructing a valid configuration?
> >
> > For everyone else, anyone deal with configuration structures and have a
> > pattern that they know about, is easy to maintain and implement, and will
> > serve the purpose of capturing and communicating the configuration? Or...
> > any thoughts on how to shape the arguments into something really easy to
> > use cross-interface?
> >
> > I think the stuff in src/stan/gm/arguments/ is almost there, but as it
> > stands now, it needs a little bit more work to make it really usable. Maybe
> > a combination of doc, tests, and factories might be enough? I'd love an
> > extra set of eyes on the code.
> >
> >
> >
> > Daniel

On Jun 24, 2014, at 6:02 PM, Allen Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:

> Hi Daniel and Bob,
>
> This looks fine from the Python side of things; Rcpp and Cython do pretty much
> the same thing.
>
> That said, I'd urge erring on side of simplicity and C idioms for maximum
> compatibility with (future) wrapping libraries. For example, using a struct or
> an enum rather than a class when it's possible seems like a good idea.

A C++ struct is just a class where everything's public.
Is there a narrower notion of struct we can invoke somehow?
You mean something without methods?  Or without virtual methods?

Enums are OK for finite sets of values, but most of our
config is nested in that you specify an enum-like decision
(e.g., HMC or NUTS, or sample vs. optimize), and then that determines
a further set of params.

So I'm not exactly sure what you mean by simple when we need
nested config, some of which takes values other than enums.

Is there something specific we need to avoid on the C++
side?

- Bob

On Jun 24, 2014, at 6:28 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> As I was saying before, this sort of testing is more circular than I want it. Maybe it shouldn't be hand-coded, but perhaps we can serialize the current valid configurations to disk now and really force someone changing the spec to be conscious and think through the changes made to this spec.

It seems to me that one of two things will happen.

1.  It's easy to update the tests, so they won't test
that things stay fixed.

2.  It's hard to update the tests, so the interfaces will
never get changed.

They will make people take a conscious step to change the interfaces,
but presumably they're doing that when they change the interfaces
anyway.

So we'd need to have something that tests current behavior, but
isn't just auto-generated.

To the extent we can make dependencies modular, we can test
those.

> The alternative is to have each interface define some intermediate object, say a configuration string matching what we input to argv in CmdStan and let the parser handle the unpacking.
>
> I would not like to use a string as the configuration. I think that's really hard to maintain.

Why?  Seems like the easiest way to do things to me.
For instance, if we have something like JSON, that seems
more portable than passing objects around through Rcpp
or other interfaces.  Not that I think it's the right thing
to do, just that it seems easiest.

- Bob

I mean if there's a programmatic way to do it, as in the way
Michael currently put things together.

>
> What do you mean by "mapping" and "general"?

By "mapping", I just meant you move among

  Stan Config <--> Python Dictionary
              <--> R List
              <--> JSON serialization

By "general", I mean that once the config object's defined,
then so is everything else.  So we can write the <---> functions
exactly once.

> The only reasonable pattern for something general and
> nested for config is the following
>
> Simple:  properties objects map string keys to values,
> where a value is either a string or another property
> object
>
> Sequence Values:  Add sequence values
>
> Numeric Values:  Add numeric values.
>
> With sequence and numeric values, we basically get something that
> could be coded as strings in JSON and would have a direct analogue
> as an R list or Python dictionary.

...

> I'm not sure the best way to nest this in C++.  A general
> approach would be to use the variant structures from Boost that
> are used in the abstract syntax tree for the parser, which has
> the same problem in that right-hand sides can be one of many
> things and you want to act differently for each.
>
> Micheal's implemented it using pointers.

That's highly sub-optimal from a type safety point of view.
But it's essentially what Java does.  The Boost variant
structures are more types safe (you can't just drop in any old
pointer), but they're a pain to use.

- Bob

I think it would make sense to refactor rstan so it is installable via devtools::install_github.  This would require copying the relevant headers into the inst/include directory and commiting them into the repository, since install_github can't do submodules (as far as i know).  But the updating can be automated, memory is cheap, and the ease of installation is significant.  Here's a branch of rstan that is installable via install_github:  https://github.com/jrnold/rstan/tree/install_github.

As I see it, the standard for R packages is be installable via CRAN, and if not CRAN, then via devtools::install_github. These days, anything else is very unusual and will probably turn off users.

On Tue, Jun 24, 2014 at 1:36 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> On Jun 24, 2014, at 7:32 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> > On Tue, Jun 24, 2014 at 1:23 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Jun 24, 2014, at 6:28 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> > >
> > > As I was saying before, this sort of testing is more circular than I want it. Maybe it shouldn't be hand-coded, but perhaps we can serialize the current valid configurations to disk now and really force someone changing the spec to be conscious and think through the changes made to this spec.
> >
> > It seems to me that one of two things will happen.
> >
> > 1.  It's easy to update the tests, so they won't test
> > that things stay fixed.
> >
> > 2.  It's hard to update the tests, so the interfaces will
> > never get changed.
> >
> > They will make people take a conscious step to change the interfaces,
> > but presumably they're doing that when they change the interfaces
> > anyway.
> >
> > So we'd need to have something that tests current behavior, but
> > isn't just auto-generated.
> >
> > Yeah, I'm out of ideas. Not sure where we should be between 1 & 2.
> >
> > I don't presume changes to the interface are conscious now.
>
> Zombie programmers?  I presume at least Marcus intended
> to change the interface to include L-BFGS options.   If other
> things changed, they need to be documented and tested, as well,
> of course.

Yes, zombie programmers. I turn into a zombie sometimes, especially when I'm refactoring. Sometimes I don't realize that my change actually has an effect until I run the tests and see the failure. So, I'm using my experience here as a guide.

I believe Marcus intended to change the interface to include the L-BFGS options. But I can't tell if the change from "> 0" to ">= 0" in arg_tolerance or changes in arg_bfgs taking tol_obj from 1e-8 to 1e-12 was intended. Just not sure what to make of it just based on the changed code.

> >
> > To the extent we can make dependencies modular, we can test
> > those.
> >
> > > The alternative is to have each interface define some intermediate object, say a configuration string matching what we input to argv in CmdStan and let the parser handle the unpacking.
> > >
> > > I would not like to use a string as the configuration. I think that's really hard to maintain.
> >
> > Why?  Seems like the easiest way to do things to me.
> > For instance, if we have something like JSON, that seems
> > more portable than passing objects around through Rcpp
> > or other interfaces.  Not that I think it's the right thing
> > to do, just that it seems easiest.
> >
> > Sorry, I really said the wrong thing. I would not like to use CmdStan's command line invocation as the string configuration. It feels a little too non-standard for me to be touting that as our public interface. But I'm happy to be out-voted here.
>
> Agreed.  I think I'd rather go with something like JSON
> that has a more conventional structure.  I was the one
> who was strongly opposed to the new interface from the get
> go, and I'm still on the fence about it.  It works better
> than I expected in practice, but it's still highly non-standard
> and hence a pain to doc.  The problem is that a more standard
> interface has all the flat dependency issues which Michael neatly
> solved with his approach, which is why I'm on the fence rather
> than way over it.

>
> - Bob
>

This would require copying the relevant headers into the inst/include directory and commiting them into the repository, since install_github can't do submodules (as far as i know).  But the updating can be automated, memory is cheap, and the ease of installation is significant.  Here's a branch of rstan that is installable via install_github:  https://github.com/jrnold/rstan/tree/install_github.
>
> As I see it, the standard for R packages is be installable via CRAN, and if not CRAN, then via devtools::install_github. These days, anything else is very unusual and will probably turn off users.

I know. I have an unpushed branch that would allow rstan to go onto CRAN and would probably work with install_github() too. We are mostly just concerned with surviving the 2.3.0 release at the moment.

Ben

messages.subject: Stan 2.3 released (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan)
messages.body_plain:
We're happy to announce RStan, PyStan and CmdStan 2.3.
Instructions on how to install at:

   http://mc-stan.org/

Release notes below.

As always, let us know if you're having problems or have comments
or suggestions.

- Stan Development Team

v.2.3.0 (18 June 2014)
======================================================================

We had a record number of user-submitted patches this go around.
Thanks to everyone!

New Features
------------
* user-defined function definitions added to Stan language
* cholesky_corr data type for Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
* a^b syntax for pow(a,b)  (thanks to Mitzi Morris)
* reshaping functions: to_matrix(), to_vector(), to_row_vector(),
  to_array_1d(), to_array_2d()
* matrix operations: quad_form_sym() (x' *Sigma * x), QR decompositions
  qr_Q(), qr_R()
* densities: Gaussian processes multi_gp_log(), multi_gp(),
  and alternative negative binomial parameterization neg_binomial_2()
* random number generator: multi_normal_cholesky_rng()
* sorting: sort_indices_*() for returning indexes in sorted order by
  value
* added JSON parser to C++ (not exposed through interfaces yet; thanks
  to Mitzi Morris)
* many fixes to I/O for data and inits to check consistency and
  report errors
* removed some uses of std::cout where they don't belong
* updated parser for C++11 compatibility (thanks to Rob Goedman)

New Developer
--------------
* added Marco Inacio as core developer

Optimizations
-------------
* turned off Eigen asserts
* efficiency improvements to posterior analysis print

Documentation
-------------
* Clarified licensing policy for individual code contributions
* Huge numbers of fixes to the documentation, including many
  user-contributed patches (thanks!), fixes to parallelization in
  CmdStan, Windows install instructions, boundaries for Dirichlet and
  Beta, removed suggestion to use floor and ceiling as indices,
  vectorized many models, clarified that && doesn't short circuit,
  clarified von Mises normalization, updated censoring doc (thanks
  to Alexey Stukalov), negative binomial doc enhanced, new references,
  new discussion of hierarchical models referencing Betancourt and
  Girolami paper,
* Avraham Aadler was particularly useful in pointing out and fixing
  documentation errors

Bug Fixes
------------
* fixed bug in lkj density
* fixed bug in Jacobian for corr_matrix data type
* fix cholesky_cov_matrix test code to allow use as parameter
* fixed poisson_rng, neg_binomial_rng
* allow binary operations (e.g., < and >) within range constraints
* support MS Visual Studio 2008
* fixed memory leaks in categorical sampling statement, categorical_log
  function, and softmax functions
* removed many compiler warnings
* numerous bug fixes to arithmetic test code conditions and messages,
  including calls from
* fixed model crashes when no parameter specified
* fixed template name conflicts for some compiler bugs (thanks Kevin
  S. Van Horn)

Code Reorganizations & Updates
------------------------------
* CmdStan is now in its own repository on GitHub: stan-dev/cmdstan
* consolidate and simplify error handling across modules
* pulled functionality from CmdStan command class and PyStan and RStan
  into Stan C++
* generalized some interfaces to allow std::vector as well as Eigen
  for compatibility
* generalize some I/O CSV writer capabilities
* optimization output text cleaned up
* integer overflow during I/O now raises informative error messages
* const correctness for chains (thanks Kevin S. Van Horn)

OK, here’s a shot.  It’s two functions; see below.  I also welcome the suggestions of Ben, Jiqiang, and others.
A

P.S.  I saw the wiki page and I would’ve put my suggestion there but I couldn’t figure out how to edit it.

foo.summary <- stan_summary(foo.fit.multiple):  returns the matrix of mean, se_mean, sd, quantiles, n_eff, R_hat (what’s currently returned in the stan print statement)

foo.waic <- stan_waic_xval(foo.fit.multiple):  returns a list of waic, elpd_waic, p_waic, elpd_loo, p_loo, pointwise, total, and se.  This function only works if one of the returned parameters in foo.fit.multiple is something called log_lik.  If there is no log_lik, it returns NULL.  We could start with the function on page 14-15 of this paper:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf

On Jun 27, 2014, at 6:03 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> OK, here's a shot.

That's a sketch of a spec, but it's a step in the right direction
for making things precise.

>  It's two functions; see below.  I also welcome the suggestions of Ben, Jiqiang, and others.
> A
>
> P.S.  I saw the wiki page and I would've put my suggestion there but I couldn't figure out how to edit it.
>

Click on the "edit" button.  You probably need to
log in to GitHub.

> foo.summary <- stan_summary(foo.fit.multiple):  returns the matrix of mean, se_mean, sd, quantiles, n_eff, R_hat

What do you mean by "matrix of"?  Are there row and column labels?
Don't you like structured objects here?  So if "Sigma" is an M x N
parameter, how do I access the summary stats for Sigma[m,n]?

> (what's currently returned in the stan print statement)

The way it works now is that stan() returns a fit object, and
that defines the behavior of the generic function print(), which
you won't find direct doc as a function for in RStan because it's
a method on the fit object.

> foo.waic <- stan_waic_xval(foo.fit.multiple):  returns a list of waic, elpd_waic, p_waic, elpd_loo, p_loo, pointwise, total, and se.  This function only works if one of the returned parameters in foo.fit.multiple is something called log_lik.  If there is no log_lik, it returns NULL.  We could start with the function on page 14-15 of this paper:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf
>

So you want a list rather than an object so you're OK with users
getting p_loo using the syntax foo.waic$p_loo or foo.waic[["p_loo"]]?

Unless p_loo corresponds to a leave-one-out cross-validation, this
seems like a confusing name.

We'll need doc for what each of these elements is.  What I really want
in all of our RStan and PyStan doc is:

argument types:  what kind of R object do you pass in?

argument content:  what is the argument?

argument constraints:  what constraints on the arguments passed in
                       are there, either singly or in conjunction.

return type:  what type of object does it return
              what is the content of that object field by field

Do you want to give them standalone names?  Names like "total" seem
a bit general.

And speaking of names, looks like you're torn between using something
like "_summarize()" that's a verb and "_summary()" which is the current
function name in R.  I'm OK with whatever we decide on naming conventions,
but we should probably stick to it.  It'd be nice if we could go with
"summarize" and "optimize" or "summary" and "optimimum" --- either describe
what it's doing or what it returns.

- Bob

out as you realize there are things you don't like.  Unless you literally
mean exactly this output is OK for you.

Should the quantiles be progammable?

Would you rather defaults other than 2.5%, 25%, 50%, etc?  If so, should

But it is a question of what you want.  With only a flat
structure, it's a pain to pull out a summary for just an array.

Should we be able to create sub-summary objects?  That is,
take a summary, give it a sequence of parameter names and
get a new summary back?  I don't know if that's how print works
or whether print gets more arguments for the things to print.

The point is that all of this needs to be specified and documented.
You can look at the existing doc now, which is pretty thorough, to decide
if things behave the way you want them to.

I'm pretty sure we're computing n_eff and Rhat with the constrained
values directly.  If that's wrong, we need a deeper rethink of what's
going on.  They are all (inverse) transforms of the unconstrained

OK --- I was just reacting to you saying you didn't want to see
the $ signs.

I think the point is that they'd be methods on an object, so you'd
doc them along with the WAIC return object, not as standalone functions.

For example, you don't see "print" documented directly when you look at the
RStan index --- you see print.stanfit.  So it'd be something like
total.waic in the index if we added a total() method to the WAIC object.
Assuming you want the return type of doing WAIC to be an object.

I have no idea what people usually do in R, what users are comfortable
with, and what's the recommended practice.

>
>> Unless p_loo corresponds to a leave-one-out cross-validation, this
>> seems like a confusing name.
>
> Yes, loo is leave-one-out cross-validation, as described in the paper.

I see --- it's "truncated importance-sampling LOO".  That's a bit of
a mouthful in a variable name.

>> We'll need doc for what each of these elements is.  What I really want
>> in all of our RStan and PyStan doc is:
>>
>> argument types:  what kind of R object do you pass in?

The point is that R's not consistent.  It uses "optimize" and "summary", which
are a verb and a noun.  The optimize function creates an list object and
the summary function returns a value that depends on what it's summarizing.

This is the same issue as logLik, which is what R calls it and what we'd need
to call it as a method in order for R's general logLik() function to work on
our fit objects the way they do on a glm() output.  We can either go with what R uses for
compatibility with R or we can try to make Stan internally consistent.

It's not a huge deal --- I'm resigned to the fact that naming can never
be made consistent because of inconsistent existing standards (at least
that's the case in Java, C++, R, and everything else I've ever used).

messages.subject_clean: tagging parts of the model for slice sampling of discrete parameters
messages.body_plain:
[moved to stan-dev]

>> From Andrew:
>> P.S.  Just a reminder:  one thing we’ve been talking about from time to time is if we want to add slice sampling for discrete variables, we will need to label the appropriate terms of the log posterior.  I’m not quite sure how we’re planning to do this (one option that we discussed is to just require duplicate code, which is ugly but could get us started.  No rush on this, I just wanted to throw it into the mix in case any of you feel it would affect our current programming decisions.

On Jun 29, 2014, at 10:51 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I don't see how to block out the log probability function
> for discrete sampling -- it's not even a hierarchy as
> different statements (and I mean statements literally as
> in programming language statement) would need to go in multiple
> cross-cutting blocks.

I agree.   It seems that we’d need to do some tagging for each discrete parameter in the model, unless we can get working my pet idea of querying the Stan program to figure out, for each discrete parameter, which computations in the program don’t depend on that parameter and thus don’t need to be recomputed or included in the gradient computation in each step.  This perhaps is related to that other idea that Ben was discussing of caching the constant terms in the probability densities so we can include the full densities (which I think will be important for many purposes) without adding much to computation time.
